scenario: AITA for no longer cooking for my roommate because he dumps condiments on everything? | Because I love cooking and (at the risk of sounding arrogant) I'm pretty good at it, I've always volunteered to be in charge of dinner when dividing up chores with roommates. I'm **not** saying my food is perfect. There are a lot of things I'm trying to improve on. But I learned to cook from two professional chefs, I don't have a lot of typical issues like under-seasoning or over-cooking food, and even when I'm living with other people that are also good at cooking I'm usually asked to prepare food 3+ nights a week. Even if I'm not incredible, I at least know what I'm doing. Since this comes up later: we have a shared food budget for staples/basic ingredients (pasta, broth, canned vegetables, flour, sugar, spices, etc). Half the time we'll split the cost of meat and fresh ingredients, half the time I pay for them myself and and accept booze, snacks (another roommate is a phenomenal baker), chores, or favors as payment. The problem is, one of my newer roommates puts condiments on everything he eats. I'm not just talking about things like hamburgers, chicken wings, mac and cheese, or anything else that normally gets condiments. I've seen him put ketchup, mayo, hot sauce, A1, or barbeque sauce on chili, steak, alfredo, fried rice, curry, pizza, red sauce, gumbo, ribs that are already covered in BBQ sauce... you get the idea. And that would be fine, I guess, but he A) does it without even trying the food first and B) completely smothers the food with them. I've tried to talk to him about this. I offered to make his favorite meals, but even stuff he says he likes prepared the way he says he likes it gets the same treatment. I've asked him to at least try the food first but he refuses. I've explained that it bothers me when I put effort into a meal and he treats it the same way he treats fast food and microwave dinners, but he said it was still being eaten so it didn't matter. I finally got frustrated and told him not to give me anything for fresh ingredients anymore because I was done cooking for him. He's been complaining to my other two roommates because his monthly expenses have gone way up (he doesn't cook at all, so he either eats out or buys prepackage meals) and saying that I'm being petty and over dramatic. My baking roommate says she agrees with my decision and the other roommate doesn't care, he just wants mealtimes to be less dramatic. AITA? I think I did plenty to meet him halfway.

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether it's right or wrong for this person to stop cooking for their roommate because the roommate puts condiments on everything. Let me break this down step by step. First, the person loves cooking and is pretty good at it, having learned from professional chefs. They usually handle cooking for roommates, and even when others are good at cooking, they're often asked to cook multiple times a week. So, they take pride in their cooking and put effort into it. Now, the issue is with a newer roommate who puts condiments on everything, regardless of the dish. This includes things like chili, steak, alfredo, etc. The roommate doesn't even try the food first and just drenches it in condiments. The person tried talking to the roommate, offering to make his favorite meals, but even then, the roommate adds condiments. They also explained that it bothers them when they put effort into a meal and it's treated like fast food, but the roommate didn't care, saying it's still being eaten. Finally, the person got frustrated and told the roommate not to contribute to fresh ingredients anymore, effectively stopping cooking for him. The roommate is complaining to others about increased expenses, and the other roommates are either supportive or indifferent. So, is it right or wrong for the person to stop cooking for the roommate? Let's think about this. On one hand, the person is putting effort into cooking, and it's frustrating when someone doesn't appreciate it or alters the meal in a way that the person finds disrespectful. It's reasonable to feel upset when your efforts are not acknowledged or respected. On the other hand, roommates often have different preferences and habits. It might be difficult to accommodate everyone's tastes, and expecting someone to stop using condiments entirely might be unreasonable. Communication is key, but if the roommate is unwilling to compromise or even try the food without condiments, it's understandable that the person feels disrespected. However, stopping cooking for the roommate might escalate the situation, especially if it leads to increased expenses for the roommate. It's important to find a balance where both parties feel respected and heard. Maybe there's a middle ground, like agreeing on certain days when the roommate can add condiments or finding alternative ways to handle the situation without completely stopping cooking for him. In conclusion, while the person's feelings are valid, stopping cooking might not be the best approach. Instead, seeking a compromise or finding alternative solutions could be more effective in maintaining a harmonious living situation.
